title: Asking for changes without breaking what already works
promise: You'll know how to save the version that works before touching anything, ask for one change at a time with a written list of what can't break, and get back to the good point in under a minute the day something goes wrong.
why: Álvaro runs a surf school in Somo and built a page with Claude showing the class calendar and a WhatsApp booking button. It worked. Then he wrote: "make it more modern, change the colors, add photos, put in the prices, and make it look good on mobile." What came back was a prettier page with no WhatsApp button; it took him two days to notice, and in those two days not a single booking came in. The worst part wasn't the button: it was that he no longer had the earlier version anywhere, so he spent a whole afternoon blindly rebuilding something he'd already finished.

theory.title: AI doesn't edit: it rewrites
theory.text: When you ask for a change to something it already built you, it doesn't pick up a scalpel. It rewrites the whole chunk from what it has in front of it at that moment. Today's tools try to touch only the affected part, but they decide where that part starts and ends, and when they get the boundary wrong they take out whatever was next to it. What keeps what already worked standing isn't that the AI remembers it fondly: it's that it has it in front of it and you've told it not to touch it. If the conversation has gotten long and your good version is now twenty messages back, it rebuilds it from memory, and memory here means by eye. That's why a page can come back improved and missing the piece that was making you money. It's not bad faith or a weird glitch: it's exactly how it works, and knowing that is half this lesson.
theory.analogy: It's not Word with track changes, where what you don't touch stays identical by definition. It's a scribe you hand a manuscript to, and he copies the whole thing out by hand again. Almost every page comes out the same. On some, a line drops out, and he doesn't tell you, because he doesn't know it dropped out either.
theory.example: Álvaro asked for the page to be "more modern." It came back with a different font, more breathing room, new colors, and the contact section rewritten from top to bottom. In that rewrite, the link that opened WhatsApp with his number stopped being there. The AI didn't delete it on purpose: rewriting the contact section from scratch, that link just didn't strike it as part of "modern."

theory.title: "Change everything": six requests, one result, no one to blame
theory.text: Packing six changes into one message looks like it saves time, and at the moment of writing it, it does: four minutes instead of twenty. The bill arrives later. When the new version comes back and something's wrong, you have six suspects and no way to tell them apart, because the answer comes back whole and you can't pull out change number three while keeping the other five. The only way out is to throw out all six and start over, so the sixteen minutes you saved get charged back with interest. With one change at a time, the suspect is always the same: the last thing you asked for. There's a second, less obvious reason: every request carries inside it an unwritten "and leave everything else the same" that you take for granted, and the more things you ask for at once, the bigger that "everything else" gets. And a third, purely mechanical reason: the longer the assignment, the worse the last instructions get followed, so request number six almost always comes out worse than request number one.
theory.example: Álvaro wrote six changes in one message and it took four minutes. Afterward he lost two days of bookings and an afternoon of rebuilding. One at a time, it would have been six messages of about three minutes each, eighteen minutes total, and he would have caught the missing button in minute six, with only one change to suspect.

theory.title: The good point: the only real way back is a file of your own
theory.text: Writing "go back to how it was" doesn't work, and it's worth understanding before you need it, not after. The AI doesn't keep a copy of your earlier version waiting for you to ask for it: it writes a similar one. It'll remember the big picture and lose the details, which is exactly where whatever worked used to live. The real way back is a file saved on your computer, with its own name and date, and it takes thirty seconds to make. Give it a name that says what worked: "bookings-2026-08-18-whatsapp-ok.html" will tell you in three months what "bookings-final-2-good.html" never will. Save a new one every time something starts working, not every time you touch something: good points are few and worth a lot, and a folder with forty files is the same as having none. With three or four well-named saved versions you're more than covered for any project you're starting now.
theory.analogy: It's a saved game in a video game. Nobody saves before every step down the hallway. Everybody saves before opening the boss's door.

theory.title: The sentence that protects everything: what does NOT get touched
theory.text: A well-made change request has three parts, and almost everyone only writes the first one. One, what you want changed, said precisely; two, what can't be touched, named item by item; three, how you're going to check it went well. The second one is the one that saves you, and it's the one nobody writes, because it seems redundant: "obviously the booking button stays." It's not obvious. The AI has no idea which parts of your project make you money and which are decoration; to it, the WhatsApp button and the background gradient weigh exactly the same. Naming five or six specific elements turns your assumption into its instruction, which is the only way it actually gets followed. And there's a bonus nobody expects: writing that list forces you to know which five things your project can't lose, and that's more than most people know about what they've built.
theory.example: Álvaro's well-written request: "Change ONLY the button color to dark green. Don't touch: the WhatsApp button or the number it links to, the class calendar, the prices (€35 for a single class and €120 for the four-class pass), the email form, or how it looks on mobile. If changing the color would require touching anything on that list, stop and tell me before doing it."

theory.title: The check round: ninety seconds that save you two days
theory.text: The AI is going to tell you "done, changed it" whether it is or isn't. It's not lying to you: it's confirming it wrote what it meant to write, not that your page still works, because it doesn't use it. You're the one who uses it. Write the list of six or eight things that need to keep working once, and run through the whole thing after EVERY change, even one that seems trivial, because trivial-looking changes break things just as much as big ones. Always start with what you did NOT ask to change: that's where the damage is, not in what you did ask for, which you can just glance at. Check it on mobile too, because more than half the people who'll visit your page will come from a phone, and some breakages only show up there. Ninety seconds a round, stopwatch in hand. Álvaro's two days without bookings would have been saved by item number one on that list.
theory.example: Álvaro's list, pinned in a note on his phone: 1) press the WhatsApp button and it opens WhatsApp with the correct 6XX number typed in; 2) the calendar shows this week's classes, not May's; 3) it says €35 and €120; 4) I fill in the form, hit send, and the thank-you message shows up; 5) on mobile I don't have to scroll sideways; 6) the photos show up, no broken image icons.

theory.title: The two-attempts rule, and how to get out of a poisoned chat
theory.text: If you've asked for the same change twice and it still isn't coming out right, stop asking. By the third time you're not correcting anymore: you're stacking up bad answers that stay written in the conversation and drag everything that comes after toward the same mistake. The sign is unmistakable and it's this: the fourth answer looks more like the first one than like what you just asked for. There are two ways out, and both start the same way, going back to the good point. The fast one: edit your own message — hover over it and a pencil icon appears, on mobile hold your finger down on it — and the conversation rebuilds from there, so the bad answers stop counting; nothing gets deleted from your account, both branches remain and you jump between them with the little arrows that show up next to it. The good one, once the chat is already twenty or thirty messages in: open a new one, paste the good-point file, paste the list of what needs to keep working, and ask for the change again, worded differently, not repeated. A new chat with the good file inside performs much better than an old chat with forty messages of history piled on top.
theory.analogy: It's the exact moment you stop arguing with someone who misunderstood from minute one and say "wait, let me start over." It costs less than continuing to qualify on top of what's already been qualified.

tasks.title: Pull out the complete file and save it as your good point
tasks.where: In the Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini app, in the chat where you have something that already works
tasks.action: Before asking for any change, get yourself a copy. Paste the message below, wait for the code block, and click the "Copy" button that appears at the top right of the block. Create a folder on your desktop called "versions" and inside it an empty text file (on Windows: right-click on the folder, "New" and "Text Document"; on Mac: TextEdit, then the "Format" menu and "Make Plain Text," because otherwise it saves it with formatting and it won't work). Paste it in, save, and rename the file with the date and what works, like this: bookings-2026-08-18-whatsapp-ok.html
tasks.prompt:
Give me the complete file exactly as it stands right now, in a single code block, from start to finish.

Don't summarize it. Don't put "(the rest stays the same)", or "...", or comments like "here goes your previous code". I want to be able to copy it, paste it into an empty file, and have it work without touching absolutely anything else.

Below the block, on a single line and outside the code, write what this version does, so I can name the file.
tasks.expect: A long code block with a "Copy" button above it and, below it, a short sentence like "Booking page with calendar, prices, and WhatsApp button." On your desktop, a file that opens in the browser when you double-click it and looks the same as it does in the chat.
tasks.stuck: If "... (rest of the code stays the same)" shows up in the middle of the block, don't save it: it's incomplete and won't work as a way back. Reply "you cut it off, give me the whole thing, no ellipses and no comments about the rest staying the same." If opening the file shows you the code instead of the page in the browser, the file is still named .txt underneath: on Windows open File Explorer, go to the "View" tab, check "File name extensions," and rename it removing the .txt at the end.

tasks.title: Write the list of what already works
tasks.where: In the same chat, right after saving the file
tasks.action: You're going to use this list after every change for months, so it deserves ten minutes. Ask the AI for a draft, because it sees the whole page and you'll miss things, and then correct it yourself, because it doesn't know which parts make you money. Once you have it, save it in a note on your phone or in a text file next to your versions.
tasks.prompt:
Look at the version we just settled as good and make me the checklist I'm going to run through every time I ask you for a change.

I want between 6 and 10 items. Each item has to be something I can check in under fifteen seconds by opening the page: pressing something and seeing what happens, or reading a piece of data and seeing if it's the right one.

Nothing like "the design is coherent", "the user experience is good", or "the code is clean". I can't check that and it's no use to me.

Write them as imperatives in this exact form: "Press X → Y should happen".

Order them putting first whatever would cost me money or clients if it stopped working, and decoration at the end.

If there's something on the page you don't know the purpose of, don't make it up: put it aside at the end and ask me about it.
tasks.expect: A numbered list of 6 to 10 concrete checks, with the button or piece of data that your project depends on at number 1. Read it all through carefully: something important that only you know is almost certainly missing, and some decorative item is probably extra. Add and remove by hand until the list is yours.
tasks.stuck: If it gives you things like "verify that the interface responds correctly," tell it: "I can't check this. Rewrite it telling me exactly what I press and what I should see on screen." If your project isn't a page yet but a text, a spreadsheet, or an assistant, that's fine too: the list becomes "what needs to still be there and with what content."

tasks.title: Ask for a single change with the list of what doesn't get touched
tasks.where: In the same chat, with the good point already saved
tasks.action: This is the template you're going to use for the rest of your life with these tools. Copy it and fill in the brackets. One single change, no matter how tempted you are to make the most of the trip. And name five specific things in the list of what doesn't get touched: if you write "don't touch anything else," you're not naming anything and it doesn't protect anything.
tasks.prompt:
I want a single change. One. If improvements occur to you along the way, don't make them: note them at the end in a list and I'll decide later whether I want them.

THE CHANGE:
[WRITE ONE SINGLE THING HERE, as specific as you can. Bad: "improve mobile." Good: "on mobile the menu overflows to the right and you have to scroll sideways; I want it to fit without scrolling"]

WHAT DOESN'T GET TOUCHED, item by item:
- [ITEM 1, for example: the WhatsApp button and the number it links to]
- [ITEM 2]
- [ITEM 3]
- [ITEM 4]
- [ITEM 5]
And also not: text, prices, links, or names of anything, even if you spot typos.

IF THERE'S A CONFLICT: if making the change would require touching something on that list, stop and don't do it. Tell me what would need to be touched and why, and wait for my answer.

WHEN YOU'RE DONE, in this order:
1. The complete new version, whole, no ellipses.
2. Below it, the list of everything you changed, line by line, including anything you touched that I didn't ask for.
3. Below that, what I should check to know whether anything broke.
tasks.expect: The new version, a short list of changes, and a checklist. If item 2 has a single entry and it matches what you asked for, you're good. If it has seven, you have six things to check before accepting anything.
tasks.stuck: If it ignores the "don't touch" list and rewrites half the page, don't argue inside that chat: go back to the good point (task 7) and ask again with the change split into two smaller halves. A change the AI can't make without touching five things is almost always a change you described too broadly.

tasks.title: Ask what it touched before you look at anything yourself
tasks.where: In the same chat, as soon as the new version arrives
tasks.action: Resist the urge to open the page and see if it's prettier. First make it confess. If it already gave you the changes list with the previous template, read that and skip to the next task; if it didn't, or gave you a vague summary, paste this.
tasks.prompt:
Before I look at anything, tell me exactly what you touched.

A list, one item per change, in this form:
WHAT: ... / BEFORE IT SAID: ... / NOW IT SAYS: ... / WHY: ...

Include EVERYTHING, including anything you changed that I didn't ask for: names, order of things, sizes, spacing, text, links.

If you removed something, write the word "removed." Don't hide it inside "simplified" or "reorganized."

If you truly haven't touched anything besides what I asked for, answer only with this sentence and nothing else: "Only what you asked for, one change."

Don't explain the code to me or tell me about your design decisions. I only want to know what's different from the previous version.
tasks.expect: A short, concrete list, or the sentence "Only what you asked for, one change." When you asked for one thing and the list has seven, you already know where the problem is going to come from: review those six extras one by one before accepting anything.
tasks.stuck: If it answers with vague stuff ("I improved the structure and optimized the styles"), push back: "I don't want a summary. Tell me what it said before and what it says now, point by point." If it still can't, it's rewritten so much it doesn't even know what was there: go back to the good point and ask for the change again, smaller.

tasks.title: Run the check round on the computer and on mobile
tasks.where: In your browser and on your phone, with the list from task 2 in front of you
tasks.action: Open the new version and go through the list from top to bottom, item by item, marking good or bad. Start with what you did NOT ask to change. Then open it on mobile: if it's a Claude artifact or a ChatGPT canvas, open the same chat from the mobile app; if it's a saved file, email or WhatsApp it to yourself and open it from there. Time yourself: it should be ninety seconds, not ten minutes.
tasks.expect: The six or eight items checked off. It's normal for one out of every three or four rounds to turn up a problem, and almost always in something you didn't ask to change. Catching it here, thirty seconds after the change, is free; catching it two weeks later costs an afternoon and, if the page is published, costs clients.
tasks.stuck: If something's broken and you don't know how to describe it, take a screenshot and upload it to the chat with the paperclip icon to the left of the text box: all three assistants read images. And if it breaks on mobile but not on the computer, say so in those exact words, because they're two different problems and the AI won't guess it.

tasks.title: Cause the disaster on purpose, with a safety net underneath
tasks.where: In the same chat, and only if you already have the good file saved on your computer
tasks.action: You're going to see with your own eyes why "change everything" doesn't work, somewhere it costs you nothing. First check that the file from task 1 is saved and opens fine. Then send the message below exactly as written, with no added protection, and as soon as the new version arrives run your whole checklist.
tasks.prompt: Change everything: make it much more modern, with a different style, different colors and different fonts, better structure, more professional, and looking great on mobile. Reorganize whatever needs it.
tasks.expect: A noticeably prettier version at first glance. When you run the checklist, it's typical for one to three items to have dropped: a link that no longer goes anywhere, a price that got lost along the way, a form that no longer sends anything, a text that turned into "Lorem ipsum." There's the lesson, on your own page, without having lost a single client.
tasks.stuck: If by chance nothing broke, don't switch methods: you got lucky today. If you want to really see it, chain three "now improve it more" messages in a row without checking anything in between; by the third round few pages come out whole. And remember this only works because you have the good point saved: without a saved file, don't do this exercise.

tasks.title: Get back to the good point in under a minute
tasks.where: In a NEW chat, not the one you just wrecked
tasks.action: Don't ask it to "go back to the earlier version," because it'll write you a similar one, not the same one. Open your saved file with Notepad (right-click, "Open with," "Notepad") or with TextEdit on Mac, use the "Edit" menu and "Select All," copy it, open a new chat, and paste the message below with the file inside. This boring and this effective: sixty seconds.
tasks.prompt:
This is my project's good file. It's the version that works and it's the only valid starting point. Forget any other version we've talked about.

Work ONLY from this file. Don't reorganize it, don't modernize it, don't optimize it, and don't change absolutely anything I don't ask for.

Just confirm with the word "received" and wait. Don't do anything until I ask for a specific change.

---
[PASTE THE ENTIRE FILE HERE]
---
tasks.expect: A short "received" and nothing else. From here you go back to task 3 and ask for one change, and only one, with its list of what doesn't get touched.
tasks.stuck: If it hands back the file "improved" without you asking, or throws three paragraphs of suggestions at you, cut it off with "I didn't ask for changes, wait." If the file is too long to paste, upload it as an attachment with the paperclip next to the text box. And if it still won't fit, that's the sign your project no longer fits in one conversation: that gets fixed by splitting it into several files, which is a topic for later.

tasks.title: Use the app's version history
tasks.where: In Claude's artifact panel, or in ChatGPT's or Gemini's canvas
tasks.action: When something has changed several times, the app saves the earlier versions. In Claude, at the bottom of the panel showing your page, a counter like "Version 3 of 5" shows up with two arrows to move around. In ChatGPT, inside the canvas, look in the bottom right corner for a clock icon with a spinning arrow: it opens the history. Move two versions back, look at how it was, and go forward again with the opposite arrow.
tasks.expect: Seeing your project exactly as it was two changes ago without having written a single message. Going back doesn't erase anything that came after: the right arrow takes you back to the latest version.
tasks.stuck: If you don't see the arrows, there are three possible reasons: there's only one version, the panel is showing the code instead of the preview (look for the "Preview" and "Code" tabs above the panel), or your app doesn't have this yet. Either way: this is a convenience, not a backup. That history lives inside the chat, so the day you open a new chat or delete the conversation, it's gone. Your saved file isn't.

tasks.title: Move to a new chat without losing what you've learned
tasks.where: In the old chat, once it hits thirty messages or two failed attempts in a row
tasks.action: Before abandoning it, get what it knows out of it. Paste the message below in the old chat and copy what it gives you back. Then open a new chat, paste the good file first (task 7), and then this handoff. What you're leaving behind are the bad answers that were dragging the conversation toward the mistake.
tasks.prompt:
Let's leave this conversation here. Write me the message I'm going to start a new chat with on this same project.

It has to include, in this order and with these headings in capital letters:

1. WHAT I'M BUILDING: two sentences, with my real details.
2. WHAT ALREADY WORKS AND DOESN'T GET TOUCHED: the checklist, as-is.
3. DECISIONS ALREADY MADE: things that shouldn't be revisited (colors, text, structure).
4. WHAT WE TRIED HERE AND DIDN'T WORK: what I asked for, what happened, and why we think it failed. One line each.
5. THE CHANGE THAT'S STILL NEEDED: just one, the next one.
6. HOW I WANT YOU TO RESPOND: one change at a time, list of what was touched at the end, no improvements I didn't ask for.

300 words max. Don't add anything we haven't talked about here. Don't include the code: I'll paste that separately.

Give me the text ready to copy, with no comments of yours around it.
tasks.expect: A block you can copy whole. Item 4 is the most valuable of all: it's what stops the new chat from repeating the same mistake you just went through.
tasks.stuck: Read it before pasting it and remove anything you didn't say: if a piece of data shows up that you never gave it, it just made it up on the spot. If it comes out huge or repetitive, tell it "trim it to 200 words, removing anything that doesn't change a decision." And if the old chat is so lost that even the handoff comes out wrong, write it yourself by hand in five lines: it's still much better than starting from a blank page.

matters: Saving the good point BEFORE touching anything. "Go back to how it was" isn't a way back: the AI doesn't keep your earlier version, it writes a similar one, and the details lost along the way are exactly the ones that made it work. Without a file of yours with a date in its name, every change is a jump with no net, and the day it fails you it costs a whole afternoon to rebuild something you'd already built.

One change per message, no exceptions. Six requests at once give you six suspects and a single answer that can't be taken apart piece by piece, so the only possible fix is to throw the whole thing out. One at a time, the culprit is always the last thing you asked for, and you catch it the very next minute.

Writing item by item what doesn't get touched. The AI can't tell the button that brings you customers from the background gradient: both are just text to it. Naming five specific elements turns your assumption into an instruction; writing "don't touch anything else" names nothing and so protects nothing.

Running the checklist after EVERY change, starting with what you didn't ask to change. The AI's "done, that's it" means it wrote what it meant to write, not that your project still works. You're the one who checks that, and it's ninety seconds that save you the two days Álvaro went without a single booking.
ignore: Git and branches. It's the professional way to save versions and someday you'll want it, but it lives in the terminal and has its own learning curve. A folder with three or four dated files does ninety percent of the work for you today, and you don't need the other ten percent yet.

Automated tests, meaning programs that check your program on their own every time you change something. They're great when your project has many pieces and many people. With one page and a checklist of eight items you run in ninety seconds, you're better served and you learn more about what you have.

Numbering versions with those three digits you see in serious software, like 2.4.1. It's a language meant to warn other people whether a change is going to break something for them. As long as you're the only one using your project, the date in the filename says more and there's nothing to learn.
canDo: Respect a "don't touch" list fairly well, as long as you write it item by item and in the same message as the change, not three messages earlier.
Tell you what it touched if you ask with those exact words, including what it changed without being asked. It's one of the things it's surprisingly honest about when asked directly.
Work from scratch on a file you paste in whole, without needing anything from earlier conversations. That's why a new chat with your good point inside is such a good place to start.

Repeat the same small change fifteen times without getting tired, without taking offense, and without getting worse. You can ask for ten variations of a button and the tenth will be as good as the first.
cantDo: Give you back the earlier version exactly as it was. It doesn't keep it saved anywhere: it rewrites it from memory, and in that rewrite what didn't seem important gets lost, which is usually the important part.

Know which parts of your project make you money. To it, the booking button and the background color weigh exactly the same, and it'll decide which one to sacrifice based on criteria that have nothing to do with your business.

Check that your project actually still works. It doesn't open your page, doesn't press your buttons, doesn't fill in your form, and doesn't look at it on a phone. When it says "done," it's talking about the text it wrote, not your business.
Warn you that it deleted something if you don't ask. It's not hiding it on purpose: to it, a rewritten section is just a rewritten section, and it doesn't keep track of what got left out.
words: The panel that opens on the right in Claude and shows you, working, what it just wrote: the page, the app, the sheet. What you see there actually works, the buttons can be pressed.
The same idea in ChatGPT and Gemini: a separate window, next to the chat, where your text or your page stays fixed and gets edited there, instead of being repeated in full in every reply.
The list of times something has changed, saved one by one, with arrows to go back and see how it looked before. It lives inside the chat, so it disappears if you delete the conversation.
Your saved copy of the last time everything worked: a file on your computer, with the date and what worked written in the name. It's where you go back to when something breaks.
Something that used to work and stopped working because of a change made somewhere else. The button that disappears the day you asked to change the colors.
The detail of what was different between the earlier version and the current one, item by item. It's what you ask for when you want to know what it touched besides what you commissioned.
How far what you asked for reaches. Small means it touches one thing and you know where to look if it fails; big means it touches everything and there's no way to know what broke.
The file a web page is written in, top to bottom, in plain text you can read. If you save it with a name ending in .html and double-click it, it opens in the browser like any other page.

Everything the AI has in front of it at the moment it answers: your message and whatever was written earlier in that same chat. When your good version drops twenty messages back, it stops having it in front of it and starts rebuilding it by eye.
next: Take the project you have half-finished today, save its good point with task 1, write its checklist with task 2, and ask for the next change with the template from task 3: one, and only one, with the five things that don't get touched named by name.
